strengths: Addresses an important problem: unreliable minority-class pseudo-labels in semi-supervised graph learning. The modular combination of label agreement, ranking, and ambiguity filtering is practical and compatible with several GNN architectures.

Reports substantial improvements across multiple benchmarks and imbalance ratios. For example, Table 2 shows Macro-F1 gains of 3.77 points on Cora and 8.13 points on CiteSeer over the strongest listed baseline. Supplementary experiments extend evaluation to heterophilous graphs and ogbn-products.

Pseudo-label accuracy analyses, five-run evaluations, pseudocode, hyperparameter ranges, hardware details, and a code link provide useful support for reproducibility. No material research-ethics concerns are apparent from the described benchmark study.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 is false as stated. Minority embeddings can lie exactly at their class centers, giving D_intra = 0, while a finite-concentration vMF classifier still has positive prediction entropy. Increasing distance from the true center can also decrease entropy when a prediction becomes confidently wrong. Appendix C additionally produces mutually inconsistent upper and lower bounds when D_intra = 0 and drops the class priors used in the original model. These errors undermine a central claimed contribution.

Theorem 2 conflates labeled-class imbalance with neighborhood composition. Changing which nodes are labeled need not change cross-class neighbors or embeddings under a fixed feature extractor. No graph-generating assumptions establish the asserted relationship. Appendix D also concludes proportionality to rho after asserting proportionality to rho squared; neither scaling is justified.

The theoretical quantity and implemented filter are insufficiently connected. Definition 1 measures distance from the true class center, whereas DGIS uses the relative gap between the nearest two centers; these can disagree substantially. No approximation guarantee or direct validation establishes that DGIS mitigates the defined quantity. Theorem 3 establishes a weighting property, not a reduction in geometric imbalance, and the confidence weight min(r, 1-r) does not increase monotonically with agreement.

Experimental reporting contains consequential contradictions. Tables 1 and 32 mark both Node-Reordering and DGIS as absent in the best-performing rows, contradicting the accompanying interpretation. Tables 7 and 17 report different UNREAL results for apparently identical ogbn-arxiv settings. Claims of consistently outperforming every baseline also conflict with Table 4, where GraphSAGE Macro-F1 is 71.86 versus 73.59 for GraphENS with TAM. These discrepancies require resolution before the component claims can be trusted.

Originality relative to the closest prior work is insufficiently established. Appendix B acknowledges that M3S already filters pseudo-labels through clustering/classifier agreement, closely overlapping DPAM. M3S is compared only on CS-Random without uncertainty estimates, while the directly relevant 2025 IceBerg method is discussed but not evaluated. With the theoretical claims unsupported, the incremental methodological contribution needs stronger isolation.

The scalability evidence does not establish total computational cost. Table 12 measures fixed-epoch training and a selection operation on small graphs, while Appendix K permits 40–100 rounds with up to 2,000 epochs per subsequent round. Complete runtime and peak-memory comparisons are needed, together with clearer UNREAL configurations for ogbn-arxiv/products and comparable baseline tuning budgets.
